text: For me, yes, though it depends on one's circumstances. If someone is struggling to pay the bills, salary will obviously come first. But once basic needs are covered, enjoying your work makes a huge difference to your overall wellbeing. I know people who earn a lot but dread Monday mornings, and honestly, I wouldn't swap places with them.

tips.kk: Жұмсартатын сөздер табиғи естіледі, пікірді тым қатаң етпейді.

questions.question: Do you think job satisfaction is more important than a high salary?

text: It's given many people far more flexibility. They save hours on commuting and can organise their day around family. However, there's a flip side, because the boundary between work and home gets blurred, so some employees end up working longer than they should. Also, newcomers miss out on learning informally from colleagues. I think a hybrid model probably works best.

questions.question: How is remote working changing the way people live?

text: Not really. The job market is changing so quickly that many skills become outdated within a few years, so people will probably switch careers several times. That might sound stressful, but it also means more variety and opportunity. In my parents' generation, staying with one company was the norm, whereas young people now are far more adaptable.

questions.question: Do you think people will have a single career for life in the future?

text: I think their main job is to create the right conditions rather than create jobs directly. That means supporting small businesses with tax breaks, and investing in training so workers can adapt to new industries. Direct job creation, like public projects, can help in a crisis, but it's rarely sustainable. So prevention and retraining are probably more effective in the long term.
